name: Adelaide
lede: Adelaide is a very dark violet from Maerz and Paul's 1930 dictionary; the name is also a city and a woman's given name, and the books we hold do not say which, if either, it honors.

sections.title: A name nobody explains
sections.body:
Maerz and Paul's *Dictionary of Color* (1930) dates Adelaide to about 1850 and places it on plate 44, row K, column 11 [1]. Its neighbors on the same plate include Prelate (about 1895, plate 44 J 11) and Roman Purple (1924, plate 44 K 10) [1]. Whom or what the name honors is undocumented in the sources we hold [2].

The color books mention Adelaide only in other roles [2]. Finlay mentions the South Australian city as the seat of the administrators in the 1860s ochre wars, and as the home base of an opal dealer [3]. His notes also record that jewelers once sold garnets as "Adelaide" rubies [4]. Neither is a color name, and no book connects either to this violet [2][3][4].

sections.title: The swatch
sections.body: The swatch is very dark and muted: lightness 21, chroma 37, hue angle 308 [5]. Its nearest plain name is [[navy]], 8.4 units away, so it sits between that and [[royal-purple]], a darker, bluer cousin of [[purple]] [5]. Next to [[indigo]] it would read as the violet one [5].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: This is a rare painted color in our archive: three of 23,781 paintings, rarer than 79 per cent of the named colors [6]. Photographs of varnished, darkened paintings make very dark violets hard to tell from black, so treat even this count as soft [6].

openers: Adelaide is a very dark violet whose name nobody has explained.
Finlay records that "Adelaide" rubies were garnets, a trade label unrelated to this violet.

issues: Overstated Finlay: Adelaide was not "the center" of the ochre wars or opal trade; reworded to what the text says.
